title: Multiplying fractions by whole numbers
keyIdea: n × a/b means n copies of a/b. The parts stay the same size, so only the number of parts is multiplied: 3 × 2/5 = 6/5, not 6/15. The rule is n × a/b = (n × a)/b. When the answer is more than one whole, pack each full set of b parts into a whole: 6/5 = 1 1/5. To multiply a mixed number, multiply the wholes and the fraction part: 2 1/3 × 3 = 6 + 3/3 = 7.
familyTip: Cut a strip of paper into fifths and colour 2 of them. Ask: how much paper would 3 strips like this give us? Lay 3 strips end to end and count the coloured fifths. Then try it with pizza slices or chocolate squares: 4 people each eat 3/8 of a pizza, so how many pizzas did they eat?

visual.caption: Is each product less than 1, exactly 1, or more than 1? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stack copies of a fraction on bars, go past one whole, pack full bars into a mixed number, copy a mixed number and build target products.

kid: 3 × 2/5 means 3 copies of 2/5. Put them on a bar cut into fifths. Each copy fills 2 more fifths. 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 fifths, so 3 × 2/5 = 6/5.

The parts do not change size. They are still fifths. So only the top number is multiplied. The rule is: whole number times the top, keep the bottom. A common slip is to multiply the bottom too and get 6/15. That would make the parts smaller, which is wrong.

Copies can go past one whole. 5 × 1/4 = 5/4. Four quarters fill a whole bar, and one more quarter spills over. So 5/4 = 1 1/4. To write a mixed number, pack each full bar into a whole and count what is left.
For a mixed number, copy all of it. 2 1/3 × 3 is 3 lots of 2 wholes and 3 lots of 1/3. That is 6 wholes and 3/3. 3/3 is one more whole, so the answer is 7.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The National Curriculum in England (Year 5) asks pupils to multiply proper fractions and mixed numbers by whole numbers, supported by materials and diagrams. CCSS 4.NF.B.4 asks them to see a/b as a multiple of 1/b and n × a/b as (n × a)/b. Fraction times fraction comes in Year 6.

The bar model shows why the rule works. The fraction a/b is a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so n copies of it are n × a copies of 1/b. The denominator names the size of the part, and that size does not change. Turning an improper fraction into a mixed number is packing groups of b parts into wholes. For a mixed number the distributive law applies: 2 1/3 × 3 = 2 × 3 + 1/3 × 3.

Common mistakes: multiplying the denominator as well (3 × 2/5 = 6/15), which makes the answer smaller than one copy; adding the whole number to the numerator; multiplying only the whole part of a mixed number (2 1/3 × 3 = 6 1/3); and thinking that multiplying always makes a number bigger, or that a fraction answer can never pass 1. The lab makes each slip visible on the bar.

practice.prompt: {n} × 2/9 = ?/9. What is the missing top number?
practice.hint: Each copy is 2 ninths. How many ninths in {n} copies?
practice.explain: {n} copies of 2/9 is {n} × 2 = {=2*n} ninths. The parts stay ninths, so only the top number changes.

practice.hint: Draw 3 copies of 2 fifths on a bar. Are the parts still fifths?
practice.explain: 3 copies of 2 fifths is 6 fifths, so 6/5. Multiplying the bottom too (6/15) would shrink the parts, which is wrong.
{n} copies of 1/4 is {n} quarters: {n}/4. Four quarters make a whole, so this is more than 1 whole when {n} is bigger than 4.

practice.hint: How many eighths make one whole? Pack them, then count what is left.
practice.explain: 8 eighths make 1 whole, and 4 eighths are left: 1 4/8. 4/8 is the same as 1/2, so 1 1/2.

practice.hint: Copy the wholes and the third, 3 times each.

pool.hint: Read the × sign as 'copies of', then picture the copies on a bar.
Multiply the top only. The parts stay quarters.
How many groups of 4 quarters fit in 15 quarters?
pool.explain: 3 groups of 4 quarters is 12 quarters, which is 3 wholes. 3 quarters are left: 3 3/4.

pool.hint: Each copy is less than 1 whole.
pool.explain: 6 copies of something less than 1 is less than 6. 6 × 2/3 = 12/3 = 4.

pool.prompt: Tom says 3 × 2/7 = 6/21. What did he do wrong?
pool.hint: Do the parts change size when you take more copies?
pool.explain: The parts are still sevenths, so only the top is multiplied: 3 × 2/7 = 6/7.

pool.hint: Multiply the wholes and the fifth, both by 3.
Count the parts, then pack the wholes.

pool.prompt: {n} × 3/10 = ?/10. What is the missing top number?
pool.hint: Each copy is 3 tenths. Count the tenths in {n} copies.

pool.prompt: How many quarters are there in {n} × 3/4?
pool.hint: Each copy of 3/4 is 3 quarters. How many copies are there?
pool.explain: {n} copies of 3 quarters is {=3*n} quarters, so {n} × 3/4 = {=3*n}/4.

pool.prompt: Each of 4 friends drinks 2/3 of a litre of water. How much do they drink in all?
pool.hint: Work out 4 × 2/3, then pack the thirds into wholes.
pool.explain: 4 × 2/3 = 8/3. Six thirds make 2 wholes and 2 thirds are left: 2 2/3 litres.
